intro: A driver on Cicero Avenue hears a true statistic on the radio and reasons her way to a false conclusion. A committee in Philadelphia crosses out three words in a rough draft and turns a religious claim into a logical one. Eighty years later a man who escaped slavery stands before a Fourth of July audience and proves, from their own founding sentence, that their country has contradicted itself. In each case the question is the same: does the conclusion actually follow from what came before?

The first chapter gives you the tools. You will learn the difference between deductive and inductive reasoning, between an argument that is valid and one that is sound, and between a premise that is stated and one that is hiding. You will learn to name four kinds of evidence and ask each its limiting question, to read a statistic or a graph without being fooled by it, to catch the common fallacies by their shapes, and to map any argument with Stephen Toulmin's six parts: claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.

The second chapter turns those tools on the most important arguments in American history. You will read the Declaration of Independence as a syllogism, the Preamble as a single sentence of purposes, and Federalist No. 10 and No. 51 as careful reasoning from a hard view of human nature. Then you will watch Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Frederick Douglass and Abraham Lincoln argue with those texts by holding them to their own first premise. By the end you will write your own argument in dialogue with a founding document, and you will know the difference between quoting a founder and reasoning from one.
bigQuestion: How do you tell an argument that proves its conclusion from one that only sounds convincing, and how have Americans used that skill on their own founding texts?

timeline.t: Aristotle describes the syllogism in the Prior Analytics: a form in which the conclusion follows by necessity from what was stated.
John Locke's Second Treatise argues that governments exist to protect natural rights, the premise the Declaration will borrow.
Jefferson drafts the Declaration; the committee changes sacred and undeniable to self-evident.
Congress cuts about a quarter of the draft, including the passage on the slave trade, and adopts the Declaration on July 4.
The Constitution's Preamble opens with We the People and lists six purposes; Madison's Federalist No. 10 defines faction.
Federalist No. 51 argues that ambition must be made to counteract ambition; New York ratifies the Constitution.
At Seneca Falls, the Declaration of Sentiments reuses the 1776 form with two words added: all men and women are created equal.
Frederick Douglass asks a Rochester audience what the Fourth of July means to the enslaved American.
Lincoln and Douglas debate across Illinois over what the Declaration's phrase all men was meant to include.
At Gettysburg, Lincoln calls equality a proposition the nation is being tested on.
Stephen Toulmin publishes The Uses of Argument, mapping real arguments as claim, grounds, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal.
Martin Luther King Jr. describes the founding documents as a promissory note the nation has not paid.

words.d: reasoning in which the conclusion must be true if the premises are true
reasoning from particular observations to a general conclusion that is probable, never certain
both valid in form and built on premises that are actually true
an unstated premise an argument needs in order to reach its conclusion
a pattern in which two things rise or fall together, which by itself does not prove cause
a mistake in reasoning that looks like reasoning
replying to a distorted, weaker version of someone's claim instead of the real one
the general principle that makes the grounds count as support for a claim
a word or phrase that states how strong or how limited a claim is
obviously true without needing proof; the Declaration's word for its first premise
Madison's term for a group united by a passion or interest that runs against others' rights or the common good
an argument that matches a new case to an accepted one so closely that denying it means denying the original

test.q: All CPS schools are closed on Labor Day; Lane Tech is a CPS school; so Lane Tech is closed on Labor Day. What kind of reasoning is this?
test.why: The conclusion is already contained in the two premises and follows by necessity.

test.q: A nurse sees forty rash patients who all ate at one festival and concludes the festival is probably the source. What makes her argument strong rather than certain?
choices: Many fairly gathered cases point one way, but the conclusion reaches past them
test.why: Induction is judged by the size and fairness of its sample; it can be strong but never guaranteed.

test.q: All fish can fly; a trout is a fish; so a trout can fly. Which label fits?
test.why: The form forces the conclusion, but the first premise is false, so the argument is valid and unsound.

test.q: Most crashes happen near home, so driving near home is the dangerous part. What hidden assumption does this need?
choices: That people drive the same number of miles everywhere
test.why: Only if driving were spread evenly would more crashes near home mean a mile near home is riskier.

test.q: A sleep researcher is quoted about school bus budgets. What is the limiting question for that evidence?
choices: Is this expert speaking within her field?
Are the two situations alike where it counts?
Does one case stand for many?
test.why: Expert testimony carries weight only inside the expert's field; budgets are outside sleep research.

test.q: Ice cream sales and drownings rise together every summer. What should a careful reader conclude?
choices: The two are correlated, likely through hot weather, and cause is not shown
test.why: Two things rising together is a correlation; a third factor, hot weather, explains both.

test.q: So you think school should start at noon and kids should learn nothing? Which fallacy is this reply to a proposal for a thirty-minute later start?
test.why: It replaces the real claim with an exaggerated version and attacks that instead.

test.q: This book is the best of the year because no other book this year is as good. What is wrong with this argument?
choices: It begs the question: the premise restates the conclusion
It equivocates on the word year
test.why: The reason is the claim in different words, so the argument goes in a circle.

test.q: In the Toulmin model, which part is usually the hidden assumption brought into daylight?
test.why: The warrant is the principle connecting grounds to claim, and it is often unstated until you look for it.

test.q: A writer states the strongest objection to her claim and answers it before the reader raises it. Which Toulmin part is she using?
test.why: The rebuttal states exceptions or answers the best objection, and it earns a careful reader's trust.

test.q: In the Declaration of Independence, what role does Let facts be submitted to a candid world play?
choices: It is the self-evident first premise
It marks the shift from asserting a premise to proving a factual one with evidence
test.why: The sentence is the hinge between the general premise about rights and the list of charges that supports the factual premise about the king.

test.q: Why does Federalist No. 10 conclude that a large republic is the best protection against faction?
choices: Because every other cure has been ruled out as worse or impossible, and many interests keep any one from becoming a majority
Because large republics have no majorities
test.why: Madison argues by elimination and then shows the extended republic dilutes any single passion.

test.q: What premise about human nature does If men were angels, no government would be necessary rely on?
choices: That officials are more virtuous than citizens
That people are not angels, so government is needed and must control itself
test.why: The false condition points to the real premise: self-interested people need a government whose parts check each other.

test.q: What did the Declaration of Sentiments and Douglass's Fourth of July speech have in common as arguments?
choices: Both rejected the Declaration of Independence
Both contested the definition of a republic
Both granted the Declaration's first premise and showed the nation's practice contradicted it
test.why: Stanton copied the form and changed the premise; Douglass accepted the premise and proved the contradiction. Both held the country to its own words.

test.q: A student opens an essay with We hold these truths to be self-evident and then moves on without using it again. What is the problem?
choices: The founders cannot be quoted in student essays
The Declaration is not a legal document
The founding text is decoration; its premise must do work in the reasoning
test.why: Quoting a founder proves nothing by itself; the essay has to show the conclusion follows from the premise.

write.prompt: Choose one founding text from this unit (the Declaration, the Preamble, Federalist No. 10 or No. 51) and write an argument that uses one of its premises to reach a claim about a question in Illinois today. State the premise fairly, add grounds from the present, and answer the strongest reply someone could make using the same text.
tips: Claim: one sentence with a qualifier that marks its edges, such as in wards that have tried it or for a two-year trial.
Premise: restate the founding text's idea in your own words so fairly that a defender of the text would nod; no straw man.
Evidence: use at least two kinds (statistic, expert, anecdote, analogy) and ask each its limiting question before you use it.
Reasoning: write the warrant that links the premise and your evidence to your claim; if a reader might doubt it, argue it with backing.
The other side: find the strongest reading of the same text against you, as Douglas answered Lincoln, and answer it on the merits.
